Want to know how to avoid major drawdowns and improve your returns in the stock market?

Understanding Stan Weinstein's Stage Analysis is a great place to start. Every stock moves through 4 stages!

One of the most important lessons I've learned from Stan Weinstein's Stage Analysis is understanding where a stock stands in its market cycle and when to buy, hold, reduce exposure, or stay away.

The framework primarily uses the 30-week moving average (roughly equivalent to the 150-day SMA), price action, volume, and relative strength.

Stage 1: Basing / Accumulation

What does it look like?
- Usually forms after a prolonged Stage 4 downtrend
- Stock stops making consistent lower lows and starts trading sideways
- 30-week moving average begins to flatten
- Price moves above and below the flattening moving average
- Selling pressure decreases, and volume often dries up

What does it mean?
- The stock is trying to establish a bottom, but buyers haven't taken full control yet. This is where I start building my watchlist and looking for improving technicals, higher lows, and signs of accumulation.

- Remember, a stock falling 50-70% doesn't automatically make it a Stage 1 base. It needs time to stabilize and build a proper structure.

Stage 2: Advancing/Uptrend

What does it look like?
- Stock breaks out above its Stage 1 base
- Breakout ideally happens on expanding volume
- 30-week moving average starts sloping upward
- Higher highs and higher lows
- Relative strength improves against the broader market

What does it mean?
- Buyers are taking control, and institutional accumulation may be supporting the uptrend.

- This is my favorite stage to own growth stocks! I generally look for Stage 1 → Stage 2 breakouts and constructive pullbacks to rising moving averages.
- The goal isn't to buy at the absolute bottom but to participate when the stock starts showing evidence of a sustainable uptrend.

Stage 3 vs. Stage 4 - This is where a lot of us make mistakes!

Stage 3: Topping / Distribution

What does it look like?
- Usually forms after a prolonged Stage 2 advance
- Momentum slows, and price starts moving sideways
- 30-week moving average begins flattening
- Price repeatedly crosses above and below the moving average
- Breakouts start failing, and selling volume may increase
- Major support levels are still holding

What does it mean?
- The previous uptrend is losing momentum, and the stock may be going through distribution.

- Stage 3 doesn't automatically mean a crash is coming. Some stocks consolidate and resume their uptrends.

- For me, this is where I become cautious, tighten risk management, consider trimming positions, and avoid aggressively adding exposure.

Stage 4: Declining / Downtrend

What does it look like?
- Stock breaks below major support or its Stage 3 range
- 30-week moving average starts sloping downward
- Price trades below the declining moving average
- Lower highs and lower lows
- Short-term rallies often fail near declining moving averages

What does it mean?
- Sellers are in control, and the stock is in a downtrend.

- One of the biggest lessons I've learned is that technicals often reveal weakness before fundamentals do.

- A company can continue reporting strong earnings while its stock is entering Stage 4 because the market is already pricing in future expectations.

The biggest difference between Stage 3 and Stage 4:

Stage 3 = Sideways price action, flattening moving averages, potential distribution.
Stage 4 = Support breakdown, declining moving averages, established downtrend.

Another important thing to understand is that Stage 1 and Stage 3 can look very similar!

Both involve sideways price action and flattening moving averages. The difference is what happened before:

- Sideways consolidation after a prolonged decline could be Stage 1.
- Sideways consolidation after a major advance could be Stage 3.

My approach is simple:
Stage 1 - Build your watchlist and prepare.
Stage 2 - Look for opportunities to participate.
Stage 3 - Protect your gains and manage risk.
Stage 4 - Protect your capital and avoid weak downtrends.

Stage Analysis isn't perfect, but it's one of the most valuable frameworks I've learned in my investing and trading journey.

I use technicals to understand WHEN to participate and fundamentals to understand WHAT I'm buying.

Understanding these four stages can make a tremendous difference in how you navigate market cycles!

There's something that's been bothering me lately, and I feel it's worth addressing.

Many of you know that my account has become one of the go-to sources for educational content, especially during market drawdowns, along with technical and fundamental analysis. That's something I genuinely take pride in.

Throughout this year, I've spent countless hours researching, analyzing markets, and creating educational content using hand-sketched, whiteboard-style illustrations to simplify complex concepts.

Recently, several friends, including some well-known accounts in the trading and investing community, have reached out after noticing how closely certain educational content resembles my work, especially my hand-sketched visual presentations.

And I've noticed it myself, not just in the visuals, but also in how concepts are explained and presented.

I'm not here to point fingers, but it's genuinely disappointing to see work built on years of learning and countless hours of creativity being replicated with little originality.

Did I invent the hand-sketched style? Absolutely not. But I've developed my own approach, combining educational research with a consistent visual style many of you recognize today.

I have no problem with people taking inspiration from others. That's how we all learn and improve.

But take that inspiration and develop your own creative approach instead of simply copying someone else's work.

I'm an investor and trader first. Creating educational content is something I'm passionate about, and I'll continue sharing what I've learned to help others improve.

You might copy my work. You might imitate my style. But you can never copy the creativity, research, and thought process behind it.

Retail investors are doubling down on Nvidia.

Venu@Venu_7_
14:00 SGTInvesting
One of the biggest mistakes investors and traders make is confusing a stock getting cheaper with a stock becoming a better opportunity.

A gap up and a gap down can both reveal institutional activity. But they often tell very different stories.

Gap up on heavy volume, in a leader, out of a base:
- Strong earnings and institutional demand can fuel sustained buying.
- Big funds often build positions over days or weeks, not just one session.
- The gap-day low becomes an important risk-management level.
- Power Earnings Gaps (PEGs) breaking out of Stage 1 bases can mark the beginning of powerful Stage 2 uptrends.

Gap down on heavy volume:
- Can signal significant selling pressure and institutional distribution.
- Overhead supply can limit recovery attempts.
- A stock being down 30%, 50%, or even 70% doesn't automatically make it cheap.
- Weak stocks can remain weak much longer than we expect.

I know a lot of people on FinX love buying gap downs, and I don't blame them. That's their approach, and I respect it.

But my framework combines Stage Analysis and CANSLIM. I prefer focusing on gap ups backed by strong fundamentals, institutional demand, and leadership in the right sectors.

I'd rather buy strength with confirmation than get married to a stock, keep buying gap downs, and hope it eventually recovers.

Of course, not every gap up succeeds, and not every gap down leads to further weakness. Context, valuations, and risk management still matter.

The goal isn't to buy the cheapest stock. It's to identify potential market leaders and participate in their strongest trends.I'd rather miss the first 10-20% of a new uptrend than spend months waiting for a broken stock to recover.

$ABCL I asked @bot to make a chart of AbCellera’s open market insider buys over the years.

I see 6 instances over the past four years where Carl dropped between about $700k-$1M on shares. It almost seems like it’s scheduled - like he’s taking his salary + bonus and dumping it into the stock or something. Whatever the reason is, I’ll take it. You love to see insider buying.

It’s interesting to see all the buying during 2022. Management was bullish, which makes sense since they were profitable with the COVID drugs at that time. Stock was around the same price that it is today.

Also, those two buys in Q3’24 and Q1’25… the stock was close to $2.00. It was psychologically tough as a shareholder. There was hardly any news other than knowing 575 and 635 would be entering the clinic soon and that the GMP facility was being finished up. Abbvie collab announcement was exciting but did nothing for the stock. Low volume. Management was always tight lipped on calls. Those insider buys helped keep shareholders sane.

Also notice there has only been one instance of insider selling since going public, and it was all in a single quarter after the IPO lockup. They got the bag, which they deserved. Zero selling since - only buying.

Something to consider though is how much they made during that sale. For example, Carl sold nearly $150M in stock. So when he drops $1M on some shares, it’s a negligible amount of his net worth. It does add up over time though. I think he’s bought over $20M in shares since.

Michael Hayden’s purchase in Q3 seems most notable. Don’t know his net worth but I’d say that $1M in purchases were probably the most noteworthy out of all relative to his net worth. Was right after the ph2 readouts. Love to see booth buying, too.

Carl must now own over 21% of the whole company. That’s a founder with real skin in the game.

$CBRS had a killer earnings! Up 15% AH.

Cerebras just put up the kind of quarter that makes me look at the name differently.

Core revenue came in at $230.9M against ~$215M expected, up 70% from a year ago.

The real story is cloud. Cloud and services revenue grew 265% to $141.9M and is now about two-thirds of the business, while hardware sales fell 29%. Cerebras is turning into an inference cloud that also sells systems.

RPO sits at $26.1B, roughly 27x this year’s guided revenue already under contract.

They raised FY26 core revenue to $940M–$960M against $887M expected, and guided Q4 to $310M–$330M against $271M.

Q4 core gross margin is guided to 47%–49%, with core operating margin around breakeven. The losses are closing fast.

They have 700 MW of capacity under contract for delivery by the end of 2027, and the CEO said he expects revenue to triple next year.

GAAP is still messy. Revenue of $210.8M came in a hair light and EPS was −$0.67. The headlines will focus on that, but the backlog and the guide are what move this stock.

Inference is where AI spend is heading, and Cerebras was built for exactly that.

The stock is now down 70% after it's IPO, but we could be finally seeing it form a bottom.

Bullish!

One of my biggest lessons from 2026:

It's not just about how much you make during a rally. It's about how much you protect when the trend changes.

Semiconductors were responsible for a significant portion of my returns this year. But recognizing the warning signs and reducing exposure helped me protect roughly +60% YTD during this correction.

Throughout 2026, I've taken approximately 50 trades, averaging around 5 positions per month. Nearly 40% of those trades were in semiconductors and AI-related names.

That should tell you how heavily I participated in this sector and why recognizing the warning signs became so important.

Here's how it all played out.

1) The first warning sign came from $NVDA.

NVIDIA attempted a breakout but failed to sustain it. When one of the most important market leaders starts showing cracks, I pay attention.

2) The second warning was even more concerning.

Many semiconductor stocks were building the right side of their bases, looking like they were preparing for another leg higher.

Instead, we started seeing failed breakouts, sharp gap-downs, and deteriorating price action across the sector. That's when I started reducing my semiconductor exposure rather than buying dip.

Here are my semiconductor and AI infrastructure trades from 2026, including winners and losers:

$MRVL: +173% (final exit), +113% (first trim)
$ARM: +155% (final exit), +98% (first trim)
$MU: +146%
$NBIS: +60%
$TSEM: +33%
$TXN: +29%
$FPS: +25%
$ASX: +18%
$NVDA: +7%
$VICR: +4% and -9% (separate trades)
$KLAC: -9%
$STM: -9%
$CBRS: -9%
$P: -10%
$FORM: -34%
$VSH: -48%

Not every trade worked. I took losses, made mistakes, and certainly could have managed some positions better.

One exit I'm particularly happy with is $NBIS. I sold around $158 after it lost its 200-day SMA, locking in approximately 60% gains. Could I have sold into strength earlier? Absolutely, and that's one thing I could have done better.

So what's my plan now?

Over the past month, I haven't initiated any new semiconductor positions.

Instead, I've been focusing on hyperscalers like $MSFT and $META, along with $SPOT in digital streaming and $ISRG in healthcare and surgical robotics.

I'm looking for companies with strong fundamentals, constructive technical structures, and relative strength rather than forcing trades in a damaged sector.

And here's something I want to emphasize:

Many semiconductor leaders are technically broken charts. This is coming from someone who generated a significant portion of this year's returns from the sector.

I still believe many semiconductor companies have excellent long-term fundamentals. But strong fundamentals alone won't prevent a stock from entering a Stage 4 downtrend.

Many of these names need time to complete their Stage 4 declines, establish Stage 1 bases, and eventually transition back into Stage 2 uptrends.

That process could take weeks or months. Nobody knows exactly how long.There's no reason to stand in front of a moving train just because stocks are trading significantly below their highs.

Let the selling pressure ease, let the bases form, and let the technicals improve. We'll have opportunities again when the sector starts showing signs of accumulation.

My biggest takeaway:

You don't need to catch the exact bottom or sell at the exact top to make meaningful returns.

Follow the trend, respect the warning signs, manage your risk, and protect your capital when conditions deteriorate.

That's what Stage Analysis and disciplined position trading are all about.
Venu @Venu_7_ · 13 Oct 2026, 11:57 SGT
Sharing some of my thoughts on the recent weakness across AI and semiconductor names.

One thing I've always believed is that technicals often tell us about strength or weakness before the fundamentals and headlines catch up.

Looking at the broader semiconductor and memory theme, the recent price action is becoming concerning. I was expecting memory & semi stocks to build the right side of their bases, but looking back, the weakness we saw around June-July may have been an early warning sign.

We had a decent bounce over the last three months, but instead of building stronger bases, several names are now testing or losing their 50-day and 100-day moving averages.

On top of that, $NVDA is showing signs of a failed breakout, while $TSM, $SMTC, $NBIS and $LITE have also seen failed breakout attempts. Meanwhile, $AVGO has slipped below its 200-day SMA.

When stocks spend months consolidating, you want to see accumulation, higher lows, improving relative strength, and eventually a breakout. Instead, we're seeing failed breakout attempts, lower highs, and key moving averages being tested across multiple leaders in SemiConductor sector mainly.

One or two stocks showing weakness is normal, but when several leaders within the same theme start showing similar technical deterioration, that's something worth paying attention to.

A LOT of poor price action across semiconductor and AI names lately.

Does this mean the AI infrastructure cycle is over? Not at all! I still believe AI infrastructure has significant long-term growth potential.

But there's a difference between being bullish on a theme over the next 3-5 years and ignoring deteriorating price action in the short term.

As much as I'm bull at heart, you can't ignore what the market is telling you. Sometimes being patient and selective is just as important as being aggressive when the opportunities are there.

That being said, software, healthcare, crypto, and several other themes are holding up relatively well. Even some international markets, like Brazil, are showing encouraging signs of strength.

Just because one theme is correcting doesn't mean the entire market is falling apart. Capital can rotate from one area to another, and new market leaders can emerge while previous leaders consolidate.

The opportunities haven't disappeared. They're just not necessarily in the same places they were a few months ago!

The history books will be very kind to Jensen Huang.

Trillions in economic value created...all downstream from his visionary leadership decisions.

"Big investors are buying the dip. Retail traders are not"

Last week the S&P 500 had its worst week since April 2025, and BofA’s client data shows exactly who bought it and who ran.

The big money bought. Institutions put in $6.1B, about $4B of it through ETFs, and hedge funds were net buyers for the first time in four weeks.

Retail sold, for the fourth week in a row. They dumped $3.4B of single stocks while still putting $1.4B into ETFs.

$5.3B went into equity ETFs, the 4th-biggest week in BofA’s data, mostly broad US large-cap funds. Tech got bought for the first time in four weeks, and industrials saw their 15th straight week of outflows.

Since the April 2025 tariff shock, retail has been the one catching the falling knife.

This time retail was selling, and Thursday’s crash started with retail buying puts.

So the people who usually panic are the ones who stepped in, and the people who usually step in are the ones who panicked.

I've been a net buyer from Thursday until Tuesday.

When smart money buys what retail is dumping, I pay attention.

Bullish ⚡️

George from 🕹prodmgmt.world@nurijanian
00:34 SGT quoteTech
what is product management, if we break it down to first principles

there is an organization that exists to create value for the market it serves.

to create real value for a market, someone has to figure out what that market needs and design something that solves that need.

the solution must be something the organization can actually build and sell.

it must not conflict with the current strategy. ideally, it should clearly fit the strategy, strengthen it, or even help shape and define the strategy.

- it’s not linear; you take quite a few shots. good stuff takes time.
- it’s heavy on execution and grind, but it also has to be creative and maintain trust.
- experience and product sense matter a lot.
- work used to be done by many people. now maybe not so much, but it still requires others. someone has to lead it.

this function is key in an org, and i still think 1 orchestrator is best here (human or AI, tbc)

otherwise each function pushes into its own corner, and you never reach the bare equilibrium you need to be successful. the product has the wrong components, or gets shipped too late.

(bad product management can happen too. one person, but the wrong one, and you get the same result.)

who should be doing this role?

technically, anyone... assuming they are high-agency, analytical, creative, clear thinker and communicator, low ego, high trust and integrity, work well with others, and ideally have lots of good ideas, experience and/or at least talk to customers all day.

which is probably why companies keep looking.

$ARM

It’s been a while since I’ve taken a closer look at $ARM, but there have been some really interesting developments cooking in the background.

This week Google announced its new TPU 8i Max, the latest in its line of custom AI chips. Like TPU 8t and TPU 8i before it, it runs on Google’s own Arm-based Axion CPUs as the host, so Google’s newest AI chips are all being built around Arm, something the market seems to have overlooked.

Every TPU needs a CPU next to it to feed it data and run the work around it, which means every TPU Google adds pulls more Arm in with it.

Axion also runs Google’s regular cloud servers at up to 2x better price-performance than comparable x86 machines, and AI agent sandboxes run about 30% cheaper on it.

Arm-based servers were already more than 45% of server revenue in Q1, according to IDC, and Arm expects to pass 60% share across the top U.S. clouds by the end of 2026.

Google’s new TPUs are getting all the headlines, but don’t think for a second they’ll rise on their own. Every TPU ships with a CPU, and it’s built on Arm.

Great news for Arm.

Bullish ⚡️

Berkshire Hathaway is making a historic comeback:

Berkshire Hathaway outperformed the S&P 500 by +19.2 percentage points over the 1 month ending Thursday, its largest rolling monthly outperformance since 2010.

This also ranks as the 4th-largest such outperformance in 30 years.

By comparison, its biggest monthly rolling outperformance occurred during the 2008 Financial Crisis, at +29.6 percentage points.

As of Tuesday's close, the performance gap narrowed to +16.9 percentage points, but it still ranked as one of the largest since 1996.

This comes as Berkshire Hathaway's Class B stock has surged +13.2% over the last month, to an all-time high, while the S&P 500 has declined -3.7% over the same period.

To put this into perspective, Berkshire was underperforming the S&P 500 by -14.3 percentage points in May 2026.

Berkshire Hathaway appears strong, even without Warren Buffett as CEO.
